case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the President may remove a sitting Federal Trade Commission Commissioner at will notwithstanding statutory “for-cause” removal protections, or whether Humphrey’s Executor still permits Congress to limit removal for FTC Commissioners.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution Article II (Vesting Clause and Take Care Clause) as applied to presidential removal power; and the Federal Trade Commission Act’s provision insulating FTC Commissioners from removal except for cause (as interpreted through Humphrey’s Executor).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (President Trump and the United States) argue that FTC Commissioners exercise significant executive power such that Article II requires the President to have at-will removal authority; they contend Humphrey’s Executor is invalid, outdated, or inapplicable to the modern FTC, and that lower courts wrongly treated Humphrey’s Executor as dispositive without engaging the constitutional merits in light of intervening separation-of-powers decisions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Slaughter and others) argue that the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection is controlling and that Humphrey’s Executor squarely upholds Congress’s ability to provide such protections for FTC Commissioners; therefore the President’s attempted removal was unlawful and without legal effect, and courts should follow the longstanding precedent and related decisions sustaining independent agencies’ removal limits.
key_precedents: Glenn v. Thomas Fortune Fay (D.D.C. 2016) (quoted in the lower-court materials)
Wilcox (Trump v. Wilcox), 145 S. Ct. 1415 (May 22, 2025) (stay order referenced in amici discussion)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: the modern FTC’s investigative and enforcement posture makes Article II accountability concerns more acute under Seila Law and Collins. But as I see it, that argument goes to whether we should overrule Humphrey’s Executor—not to adopting Justice Alito’s or Justice Gorsuch’s “as-applied” narrowing, which would force unstable, agency-by-agency litigation over how much executive power is “too much,” effectively discarding Humphrey’s without saying so. Seila Law’s express preservation of Humphrey’s for multimember commissions, combined with Humphrey’s direct holding on this very FTC Act provision, makes adherence the more legitimate and administrable course absent an explicit decision to depart from precedent with a workable replacement rule. Wiener does not supply an independent basis to decide this case, but it supports the broader point (echoed by Justices Sotomayor and Kavanaugh) that Congress sometimes structures multimember bodies to protect decisional regularity, reinforcing my preference for a narrow decision on existing precedent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s central point—that Humphrey’s Executor is directly on point and Seila Law preserved it—carries weight only if that precedent is consistent with Article II’s original public meaning; in my view it is not, because the Vesting and Take Care Clauses presuppose meaningful presidential supervision, including removal, over principal officers who execute federal law. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s institutional-legitimacy and line-drawing concerns do not justify retaining an exception that rests on “quasi-” categories untethered from the Constitution’s text and history; if Humphrey’s is wrong, stare decisis cannot make it right. Wiener, invoked by Justices Sotomayor and Kavanaugh, does not move the analysis because it concerned a uniquely adjudicatory commission, whereas the modern FTC’s enforcement and policy-setting functions are quintessentially executive. If the Court believes reliance interests counsel caution, the candid and methodologically sound approach is to overrule Humphrey’s Executor or at least confine it to its obsolete factual premises rather than treat it as a perpetual carve-out from Article II.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis and administrability concern is the Respondent side’s strongest point, but it assumes Humphrey’s Executor must operate as a timeless categorical safe harbor regardless of how the FTC’s powers have evolved. Seila Law preserved Humphrey’s only as an exception justified by its premises; as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, when an agency’s predominant powers are investigative and enforcement-oriented, extending that exception beyond its rationale dilutes Article II accountability in a way Seila Law and Collins warn against. The instability objection is overstated: courts routinely assess whether an officer exercises core executive power in removal cases, and this FTC’s modern nationwide enforcement and policy-setting profile is not a close call. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Wiener does not change the outcome for me because Wiener’s adjudicatory-independence rationale fits a claims-tribunal model, not an agency that initiates coercive proceedings and sets enforcement priorities—functions for which presidential supervision is constitutionally essential.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s core point—that the FTC now exercises substantial coercive enforcement power and thus heightens Article II accountability—has real force, and I do not dismiss it. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that adopting Justice Alito’s or Justice Gorsuch’s “as-applied” functional narrowing would be an administrability disaster and an implicit overruling of Humphrey’s Executor, which Seila Law expressly preserved for multimember commissions and which upheld this very for-cause provision. Collins and Free Enterprise Fund sharpen the constitutional backdrop, yet they left Humphrey’s intact; under stare decisis and institutional legitimacy, we should not convert their general reasoning into an agency-by-agency relitigation of how “executive” an agency has become. And as Justice Jackson emphasizes, the real-world consequence of weakening removal protections here is intensified political pressure on enforcement and adjudication, with disproportionate effects on consumers and small actors who rely on evenhanded, non-whipsaw administration.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that the FTC’s modern enforcement toolkit looks far more “executive” than the Humphrey’s-era description, and Collins/Free Enterprise Fund sharpen the Article II accountability concern. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Seila Law preserved Humphrey’s Executor categorically for multimember commissions, and this case involves the identical for-cause provision Humphrey’s upheld—so an “as-applied” functional reclassification would effectively overrule that precedent without a stable, text-based limiting principle. Under a pragmatic textualist lens, I do not see a workable doctrinal rule that distinguishes “today’s FTC” from the FTC in Humphrey’s without inviting the agency-by-agency reassessments Roberts (and Justice Kavanaugh) warn would be destabilizing and incoherent. If Humphrey’s is to be revisited, Justice Thomas is right that it should be done candidly; but absent that explicit step, stare decisis and statutory coherence keep me with the Respondent here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis concern is the most serious counterweight, but it does not solve the antecedent Article II problem: Humphrey’s Executor’s “quasi-” rationale is in deep tension with our later decisions emphasizing presidential accountability when an agency wields substantial enforcement power (as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas note, Seila Law and Collins underscore that point). I do not accept that enforcing the Constitution here necessarily entails an unworkable, agency-by-agency free-for-all; the limiting principle is whether the removal protection is being used to insulate principal officers exercising core executive functions—investigation, prosecution, and nationwide enforcement priority-setting—rather than truly adjudicatory claims-tribunal work. Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Wiener does not move me because Wiener addressed a uniquely adjudicatory body whose independence was essential to fair resolution of individual claims, not an agency that combines rulemaking, investigation, prosecution, and adjudication with broad economic reach. If Humphrey’s is to persist, it must be confined to its justifying premises rather than treated as a categorical safe harbor for the modern FTC’s executive-leaning powers.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that the modern FTC exercises substantial enforcement authority and that Humphrey’s Executor relied on now-suspect “quasi-” labels, implicating Article II accountability concerns underscored in Seila Law and Collins. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Seila Law expressly preserved Humphrey’s as a categorical exception for multimember commissions, and an “as-applied” functional narrowing would force unstable, agency-by-agency line-drawing that effectively overrules a directly on-point precedent without saying so. Justice Thomas’s originalist critique may be a reason to revisit Humphrey’s forthrightly in a case that squarely asks us to overrule it with a workable limiting principle, but under an institutionalist stare decisis approach—given reliance on the FTC’s settled structure—the more legitimate course is to apply Humphrey’s to the identical statutory provision here. Wiener does not control, but it reinforces Congress’s accepted ability to insulate certain decisional processes, making the administrability and legitimacy costs of an implicit carve-out especially high.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis point is the Respondent side’s strongest: Humphrey’s Executor upheld this very for-cause provision and Seila Law said it was not overruling Humphrey’s, and I take seriously his concern that an as-applied approach could look like implicit overruling. But Seila Law preserved Humphrey’s only as an exception justified by its premises; when those premises no longer describe the agency’s operative powers, extending the exception beyond its rationale turns precedent into an atextual safe harbor. Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor warn about instability from agency-by-agency relitigation, yet the alternative—treating “quasi-” labels as permanently dispositive despite the FTC’s modern investigative and enforcement authority—conflicts with the original public meaning of Article II’s supervision principle as reinforced in Collins and Free Enterprise Fund. Wiener, emphasized by Justice Kavanaugh, does not undermine this conclusion because its decisional-independence logic fits a claims-tribunal model, not an agency that initiates coercive enforcement and sets national enforcement priorities.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s Article II critique is the most serious, particularly their point (echoed by Justice Alito) that the modern FTC exercises substantial enforcement authority and that Seila Law/Collins resist open-ended balancing once that line is crossed. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Seila Law expressly preserved Humphrey’s Executor for multimember commissions, and this case targets the identical FTC Act for-cause provision—so adopting an “as-applied” narrowing would function as an implicit overruling while substituting unstable, agency-by-agency characterizations for a workable rule. Under a progressive-pragmatist lens attentive to procedural fairness and administrability, Wiener’s adjudicatory-independence rationale (highlighted by Justices Sotomayor and Kavanaugh) matters because heightened political control over enforcement-and-adjudication structures risks arbitrary outcomes and undermines evenhanded process. If the Court is to revisit Humphrey’s, it should do so candidly and with a clear limiting principle, not by re-labeling today’s FTC as a basis to evade stare decisis.

John Roberts.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) directly upheld the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners, and stare decisis and institutional legitimacy counsel adherence absent a clear basis to overrule that settled precedent. Seila Law LLC v. CFPB (2020) invalidated for-cause protection for a single-director agency but expressly reaffirmed Humphrey’s Executor as a remaining exception for certain multimember commissions, making this case materially different from Seila Law on its own terms. Whatever the modern FTC’s assertedly greater executive character, the narrowest course is to apply Humphrey’s Executor to the same statutory scheme rather than to extend Seila Law to overrule or effectively negate Humphrey’s Executor. Accordingly, the President may not remove a sitting FTC Commissioner at will in the face of the FTC Act’s for-cause limitation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article II vests the executive power in the President and obligates him to “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed,” which requires meaningful control—including removal—over principal officers who execute federal law. FTC Commissioners exercise substantial executive power through enforcement and adjudicatory functions, and Congress’ for-cause restriction in the FTC Act unconstitutionally impairs presidential supervision of those officers. Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) rests on a mistaken separation-of-powers premise that the FTC is meaningfully “quasi-legislative” or “quasi-judicial,” and to the extent it authorizes insulation of principal executive officers from at-will removal, it should be overruled or at least confined to its facts. Consistent with modern Article II decisions recognizing that removal power flows from the Vesting Clause, the President may remove an FTC Commissioner at will notwithstanding the statutory limitation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting Clause and Take Care Clause presume that officers exercising significant executive power remain accountable to the President, which ordinarily requires at-will removal authority. Although Humphrey’s Executor upheld for-cause protection for FTC Commissioners, Seila Law LLC v. CFPB read that decision narrowly as a limited exception for multimember expert bodies said not to wield substantial executive power, and emphasized that the relevant premise is the set of powers the Humphrey’s Court understood to be at issue. The modern FTC’s broad enforcement, investigation, and competition-policy authority under 15 U.S.C. § 45(a) entails substantial executive power, making application of Humphrey’s Executor inapt and the statutory for-cause restriction unconstitutional as applied. As a practical matter, insulating principal officers who direct national enforcement priorities undermines presidential control and accountability over the execution of federal law.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) squarely upheld the FTC Act’s for-cause removal protection for FTC Commissioners, and nothing in Article II’s Vesting or Take Care Clauses authorizes this Court to disregard that directly controlling precedent simply because the Commission’s work has evolved. Seila Law LLC v. CFPB (2020) expressly reaffirmed Humphrey’s Executor as an exception for multimember commissions and refused to extend at-will removal requirements beyond the single-director context, so the President’s attempted at-will removal here conflicts with the statute Congress enacted and this Court has long sustained. Wiener v. United States (1958) reinforces that where Congress designs an adjudicatory, independent body insulated from political pressure, removal limits protect fairness and the integrity of decisionmaking—particularly important for those subject to the FTC’s enforcement regime and for consumers the agency is charged to protect. Respecting the FTC Act’s for-cause standard preserves stable, evenhanded administration of law and avoids politicizing enforcement choices that can disproportionately harm vulnerable communities.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FTC Act expressly provides that Commissioners may be removed only for cause, and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States squarely upheld that very statutory structure for the FTC as consistent with Article II. Whatever later cases have said about the limits of removal protections, this Court has repeatedly preserved Humphrey’s Executor as a continuing carve-out for multimember, bipartisan expert commissions (see Seila Law LLC v. CFPB, which distinguished rather than overruled Humphrey’s Executor, and Free Enterprise Fund, which likewise left it intact). Morrison v. Olson and Wiener v. United States further confirm that Congress may impose for-cause limits in certain institutional designs, and absent an explicit overruling, stare decisis and statutory coherence counsel following the on-point precedent here. The President therefore may not remove a sitting FTC Commissioner at will in the face of Congress’s for-cause protection.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting and Take Care Clauses assign the President responsibility for executing the laws, which presupposes meaningful control over those who wield executive power, including the power of removal. Whatever Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) said about a commission performing merely “quasi-legislative” or “quasi-judicial” functions, the modern FTC exercises substantial executive authority through investigations, enforcement actions, and binding regulatory activity, placing it on the executive side of the constitutional line. Applying Humphrey’s Executor mechanically to insulate principal officers who execute federal law would dilute political accountability and upset separation of powers, and any statutory ambiguity about the scope of “for-cause” protection should be read narrowly to avoid that constitutional infirmity. Accordingly, the President may remove an FTC Commissioner at will notwithstanding the FTC Act’s for-cause provision as so applied.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) squarely upheld Congress’s decision in the FTC Act to provide FTC Commissioners for-cause removal protection, and Wiener v. United States (1958) likewise recognized limits on at-will removal for certain multi-member bodies. Although later Article II decisions such as Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010) and Seila Law LLC v. CFPB (2020) narrowed and criticized aspects of the independent-agency framework, they expressly treated Humphrey’s Executor as an existing exception for multi-member commissions and did not overrule it. Under principles of stare decisis and institutional restraint, the Court should follow that directly controlling precedent here rather than invalidate the FTC Act’s for-cause provision absent a clear doctrinal necessity and a workable limiting principle.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting Clause and Take Care Clause vest the executive power in the President and require sufficient presidential control over officers who execute federal law; the FTC’s current statutory powers—investigations, administrative adjudication producing binding orders, and enforcement in Article III courts, see 15 U.S.C. §§ 45(b)–(c), 45(l)–(m), 57a—are quintessentially executive. Seila Law LLC v. CFPB and Collins v. Yellen reaffirm that for-cause tenure protections for principal officers wielding substantial executive power are incompatible with Article II, and Collins cautions courts against fine-grained “how much power is enough” balancing when assessing removal restrictions. Humphrey’s Executor upheld for-cause protection for FTC Commissioners on a now-contested premise that the FTC was predominantly “quasi-legislative” and “quasi-judicial,” but given the modern FTC’s execution of law and the Court’s intervening removal decisions, Humphrey’s is best read narrowly and does not control this case’s Article II challenge.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FTC Act expressly limits removal of Commissioners to specified “for-cause” grounds, and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) directly upheld that very statutory design for the FTC as consistent with Article II. Whatever tension modern removal cases create, this Court has not overruled Humphrey’s Executor, and principles of procedural fairness and stare decisis counsel that lower courts (and we) apply controlling precedent rather than treat it as implicitly displaced. The FTC’s multimember, bipartisan structure aligns with Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener v. United States (1958), and differs in constitutionally relevant ways from cases addressing novel structures like a single-director agency. Absent a clear rule overruling Humphrey’s Executor, the President’s asserted at-will removal power cannot override Congress’s valid for-cause protections here.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the President may remove a Federal Trade Commission Commissioner at will notwithstanding statutory for-cause removal protections, or whether Humphrey’s Executor still permits Congress to insulate FTC Commissioners from at-will presidential removal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution Article II (executive power and presidential control over executive officers, including the Take Care Clause) and the Federal Trade Commission Act’s for-cause removal protections for FTC Commissioners (as interpreted through Humphrey’s Executor).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the President’s Article II authority requires meaningful control over principal officers who exercise executive power, so the FTC’s modern powers and functions make Humphrey’s Executor inapplicable or wrongly decided; therefore statutory limits on removal are unconstitutional (or at least unconstitutional as applied to today’s FTC), and the President’s removal of Commissioner Slaughter was lawful.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the FTC Act expressly restricts removal to specified causes and that this scheme is squarely upheld by Humphrey’s Executor; because courts have repeatedly rejected similar constitutional challenges, the President’s attempt to remove Commissioner Slaughter was unlawful and without legal effect.
key_precedents: Trump v. Wilcox (stay order, 145 S. Ct. 1415 (May 22, 2025))

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest Article II argument: that the modern FTC exercises substantial enforcement power and thus should be subject to at-will presidential removal for accountability. But Seila Law and Collins expressly preserved Humphrey’s Executor, and Humphrey’s upheld this very FTC for-cause provision—so an “as-applied modern FTC” theory (as Justice Alito urges) would, in practice, overrule Humphrey’s without saying so, replacing a clear rule with an unadministrable functional test and undermining stare decisis and institutional legitimacy. Justice Sotomayor’s invocation of Wiener reinforces the difficulty of drawing a stable line between “adjudicatory” and “executive” functions across agencies; if the Court is to revise Humphrey’s, it should do so forthrightly in a case squarely presenting that question. On this record, the President concededly did not invoke the statutory for-cause standard, so under the statute as construed by controlling precedent, the removal is unlawful.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis point—that Humphrey’s Executor is squarely on-point and administrable rules counsel adherence—does not overcome the Constitution’s text vesting “the executive Power” in the President and the Take Care duty, which presuppose meaningful presidential control over principal officers executing the law. That Seila Law and Collins “preserved” Humphrey’s as an exception (as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize) is not an originalist justification for perpetuating an atextual carveout; at most it reflects the Court’s incrementalism, not Article II’s original public meaning. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Wiener does not move me because adjudicatory independence in a nonprosecutorial setting cannot justify insulating officials who wield broad enforcement and policymaking authority with coercive effect; if Wiener suggests otherwise, it too is in tension with Article II. If the choice is between forthrightly correcting a constitutional error and maintaining a precedent that dilutes accountability for executive enforcement, my methodology requires the former.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest point on the other side is Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis argument: Humphrey’s Executor upheld this very FTC for-cause regime, and Seila Law and Collins said they were preserving it. But that does not resolve the antecedent Article II problem where the FTC now wields sweeping enforcement and rulemaking power with coercive consequences; insulating such principal officers from at-will removal undermines the Take Care Clause’s accountability logic in a way Humphrey’s “quasi-legislative/quasi-judicial” premise cannot justify today. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern is real, yet a rule that confines Humphrey’s to genuinely adjudicatory bodies (as Wiener involved, and as Justice Gorsuch suggests) is more faithful to Article II than treating Humphrey’s as a perpetual congressional blank check for executive regulators. Because the constitutional defect goes to the structure of executive responsibility, I am not persuaded that reliance interests can carry the day where the agency’s modern functions have overtaken the rationale for the exception.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest point that Article II accountability is at its apex when an agency investigates and prosecutes, and that the modern FTC has a more overt enforcement posture than the 1935 Court described. But their proposed “as-applied” limitation would, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, operate as a functional overruling of Humphrey’s Executor while insisting it remains controlling law—without any administrable principle for when a multimember commission crosses some “too executive” threshold. Justice Alito’s argument that Humphrey’s factual premises have eroded is a serious invitation to revisit stare decisis in a case squarely presenting overruling, but it does not justify upholding an admittedly at-will removal where the President did not even attempt to satisfy the statute’s for-cause standard. On my pragmatic, rule-of-law approach, preserving predictable removal protections that support impartial enforcement and fair process—especially for those most vulnerable to politicized swings—counsels applying Humphrey’s and the statutory text as they stand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s proposed limiting rule—preserve Humphrey’s only for “genuinely adjudicatory/limited” bodies—squarely engages the Article II accountability concern, but it still cannot be squared with the fact that Humphrey’s Executor upheld the FTC’s for-cause protection for this very Commission despite its enforcement posture even then. As the Chief Justice stresses, Seila Law and Collins preserved Humphrey’s as an operative exception, and adopting an “as-applied” executive-function test would effectively overrule that precedent while claiming to apply it, creating an unadministrable regime where statutory removal protections fluctuate with judicial characterizations of agency “executiveness.” Justice Thomas is right that constitutional structure matters, but under my methodology the Court must either forthrightly overrule Humphrey’s (with a clear replacement rule) or apply it; this case, with a concededly at-will removal and no invoked cause, fits the latter. Wiener adds only that decisional independence can matter in context; it does not supply a workable doctrinal bridge for transforming a fixed statutory for-cause standard into a case-by-case constitutional balancing test.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s point is the hardest: Humphrey’s Executor is squarely on this statute and this Commission, and Seila Law/Collins did not purport to overrule it. But as Justice Thomas underscores, stare decisis cannot require us to perpetuate an arrangement that contradicts Article II’s vesting of the executive power and the Take Care duty where the agency exercises core executive enforcement authority; Humphrey’s “quasi” premises cannot be extended to insulate modern coercive executive power from presidential accountability. I do not accept Justice Kagan’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability objection as dispositive because the limiting principle is categorical rather than free-form balancing: removal insulation may persist for genuinely adjudicatory bodies in the Wiener mold, but not for principal officers empowered to investigate, prosecute, and impose binding legal consequences through enforcement and rulemaking. To the extent this confines Humphrey’s, that is not an evasion but a faithful application of Seila Law’s own description of Humphrey’s as a historically anomalous exception that must be reconciled with constitutional structure rather than treated as a license for indefinite entrenchment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch have the strongest Article II structural point: the FTC today exercises substantial enforcement and rulemaking authority, and Seila Law/Collins emphasize presidential accountability for core executive power. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, those same cases expressly preserved Humphrey’s Executor, and Humphrey’s squarely upheld the for-cause protection for this very Commission under this very statute—so an “as-applied modern FTC” carveout (Justice Alito’s proposal) would effectively overrule controlling precedent without saying so, which is not a legitimate stare decisis method and is not administrable. Wiener, raised by Justice Sotomayor, reinforces that we have historically tolerated some insulation where independence serves adjudicatory functions, underscoring that any major revision should be forthright and categorical rather than a case-by-case reclassification of “how executive” an agency has become. On this record, the President concededly removed at will without invoking statutory cause, so under the FTC Act as construed by Humphrey’s, the removal is unlawful.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest constitutional point: Article II’s original public meaning and the Take Care Clause favor presidential control over principal officers exercising executive enforcement power, and the modern FTC strains the 1935 “quasi” premises. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Humphrey’s Executor is not merely analogous—it upheld this very for-cause provision for this very Commission, and Seila Law and Collins expressly preserved it as an operative exception, which forecloses an “as-applied” theory that would effectively overrule while purporting to adhere. Justice Sotomayor’s invocation of Wiener reinforces the administrability concern: once we accept decisional-independence rationales in the removal context, we need a clear doctrinal rule, and the proposed functional line-drawing (“too executive”) is not a textualist, precedent-respecting way to rewrite a fixed statutory standard. If the Court is to correct Humphrey’s as a matter of Article II, we should do so forthrightly in a case that squarely seeks overruling; on this record, the President’s conceded at-will removal remains unlawful under the statute as construed by controlling precedent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch offer the strongest counter: that Article II’s Vesting and Take Care Clauses require meaningful presidential control over principal officers exercising core executive power, and that the modern FTC looks prosecutorial and coercive. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Seila Law and Collins expressly preserved Humphrey’s Executor, and Humphrey’s upheld this very FTC for-cause provision—so an “as-applied” narrowing (as Justice Alito proposes) would functionally convert a clear statutory protection into an indeterminate constitutional balancing test that undermines procedural fairness and invites politicized removals. Even if Wiener’s adjudicatory-independence rationale does not map perfectly onto the FTC’s contemporary mix of functions, the remedy for any Article II correction must be forthright overruling with a stable replacement rule, not recharacterization that leaves agencies and litigants guessing. On these facts, where the President did not invoke any statutory cause, the administrable and legitimacy-preserving course is to apply the statute as construed by controlling precedent and hold the removal unlawful.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FTC Act provides for-cause removal protections for Commissioners, and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States squarely upheld that precise structural choice for the FTC; absent an express overruling, that precedent remains controlling. Although more recent Article II cases have narrowed certain removal restrictions (e.g., Free Enterprise Fund’s rejection of dual for-cause layers), they have not displaced Humphrey’s Executor’s approval of a single for-cause limitation for a multimember, expert commission. Given institutional legitimacy and the Court’s repeated admonition that it alone may overrule its precedents, the narrower and more stable ground is to apply Humphrey’s Executor rather than reconsider it in this case. Accordingly, the President’s at-will removal is unlawful under the statute as interpreted by controlling precedent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article II vests the executive power in a single President and commands that he “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed,” which presupposes presidential supervision of those who exercise executive power. For-cause tenure for principal officers of the Federal Trade Commission strips the President of the ability to ensure faithful execution and is therefore inconsistent with Article II’s original public meaning, as reflected in Myers v. United States’ understanding that removal is a necessary incident of executive control. Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, which permitted Congress to insulate FTC Commissioners, wrongly carved out a “headless fourth branch” and should be overruled (or, at minimum, confined) given the FTC’s substantial executive enforcement authority today. Because the FTC Act’s for-cause restriction cannot constitutionally limit the President’s removal power over an executive officer, the President’s at-will removal was lawful notwithstanding the statute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article II vests the executive power in the President and obligates him to “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed,” which presupposes meaningful control over principal officers who exercise substantial executive power. Whatever Humphrey’s Executor upheld in 1935 for an FTC described as exercising “quasi-legislative” and “quasi-judicial” functions, this Court has since emphasized in Seila Law LLC v. CFPB that it has “declined to extend” Humphrey’s Executor beyond its specific context and has invalidated removal limits where they impede presidential supervision of enforcement authority. The modern FTC’s core work—bringing enforcement actions, issuing binding rules, and conducting adjudications—resembles the executive enforcement power that Seila Law and Collins v. Yellen treat as requiring presidential accountability, making the FTC Act’s for-cause protection unconstitutional as applied here. Practical consequences likewise favor a clear line that prevents Congress from entrenching powerful, policy-making enforcement officials beyond the President’s effective control.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FTC Act expressly provides for-cause removal protections for Commissioners, and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States upheld that precise statutory scheme for this multimember, bipartisan commission; stare decisis counsels strongly against discarding that settled rule in the absence of a clear conflict with Article II. Seila Law declined to extend Humphrey’s Executor to a single-director agency, but it reaffirmed Humphrey’s Executor’s continued vitality for multimember expert bodies and thus does not authorize treating the FTC as removable at will. Wiener v. United States reinforces Congress’s power to insulate certain adjudicatory/independent decisionmakers from at-will removal, which protects fair, nonpartisan administration and guards against politicized enforcement that would most harm vulnerable populations. Because the President’s attempted at-will removal contravenes the FTC Act’s text and controlling precedent, it was unlawful.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FTC Act’s text provides that Commissioners may be removed only for specified causes, and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States squarely upheld that exact statutory protection for this Commission. Whatever tension later Article II removal cases create, the Court has repeatedly treated Humphrey’s Executor (and Wiener) as a continuing carveout for multimember, expert commissions with mixed functions, and I would not overrule or effectively nullify it on an as-applied theory without a clearer doctrinal basis and attention to reliance and workability. Here the President admittedly did not invoke any of the Act’s for-cause grounds, so the removal conflicts with the statute as written; absent a direct holding overruling Humphrey’s Executor, we should enforce Congress’s chosen removal standard. Any broader reassessment of independent-agency structure is better addressed through the usual process of precedent-based increment rather than collapsing a longstanding statutory regime by recharacterizing the FTC’s functions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article II vests “the executive Power” in the President and obliges him to “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed,” which historically presupposes meaningful presidential control over principal officers who wield substantial executive power. Whatever Humphrey’s Executor v. United States permitted for the FTC as it then existed, this Court’s modern Article II cases—especially Seila Law LLC v. CFPB and Collins v. Yellen—reaffirm that for-cause insulation that strips the President of adequate supervisory authority is constitutionally suspect, and the FTC today exercises core executive power through investigations, binding administrative orders, and enforcement actions under 15 U.S.C. §§ 45(b)–(c), 45(l)–(m), 57a. Given that FTC Commissioners are principal officers (see Edmond v. United States; United States v. Arthrex), the statute’s for-cause restriction cannot be squared with the Constitution’s original allocation of executive power, at least as applied to the modern Commission. Accordingly, the President’s at-will removal was lawful notwithstanding the FTC Act’s purported limitation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FTC Act expressly provides for-cause removal protections for Commissioners, and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States upheld that precise statutory scheme for the FTC, distinguishing multi-member expert commissions from purely executive officers under Article II. Even if later cases (e.g., Seila Law) have emphasized the President’s general removal authority, they have treated Humphrey’s Executor as a narrow but still-binding exception for traditional multi-member independent commissions, reinforced by Wiener v. United States. Given stare decisis, history and tradition of independent commissions, and the significant institutional costs of overruling a nearly century-old precedent on which Congress and the Executive have long relied, I would adhere to Humphrey’s Executor absent a square holding from this Court overruling it. On that basis, the President’s attempt to remove an FTC Commissioner at will was unlawful under the statute as interpreted by binding precedent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FTC Act’s text provides for-cause removal protection for Commissioners, and Humphrey’s Executor upheld that scheme for this multimember commission; absent a clear directive from the Court overruling that precedent, we should apply it. Seila Law reaffirmed Humphrey’s Executor as a continuing exception to the President’s otherwise broad removal authority, distinguishing it from the unconstitutional single-director structure at issue there and describing Humphrey’s as covering a bipartisan, multimember body performing legislative and judicial functions. Collins likewise treated removal restrictions as generally unconstitutional when they trench on presidential control over executive power, but it did not overrule Humphrey’s Executor and instead preserved its framework as an extant carveout. Given stare decisis and the lack of a square holding displacing Humphrey’s for the FTC itself, the President’s at-will removal of an FTC Commissioner is unlawful under the statute as currently interpreted.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FTC Act provides for-cause removal protection for Commissioners, and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States squarely upheld that statutory scheme for the FTC’s multimember, bipartisan commission structure. While Seila Law LLC v. CFPB and Collins v. Yellen emphasized the President’s general Article II removal power and narrowed exceptions, they preserved Humphrey’s Executor as a continuing exception for multimember commissions and did not overrule it. Respect for procedural fairness and institutional stability counsels that changes to this long-settled arrangement—especially one repeatedly relied upon by Congress in structuring independent commissions—should come from the Court only through a clear decision to overrule precedent, not by treating the President’s at-will removal as lawful “as applied” despite the statute’s plain text. Accordingly, the attempted at-will removal was unlawful and without legal effect under the FTC Act as interpreted through Humphrey’s Executor.
